The Art of Static Fetching

By Jane Doe

Most of the web an agent actually needs — documentation, articles, encyclopedias, changelogs — is still served as plain server-rendered HTML. Reaching for a headless browser by default wastes seconds of latency and hundreds of megabytes of memory on pages that would have been perfectly readable with a single HTTP request. The pragmatic order of operations is fetch first, render only when fetching demonstrably failed to produce content worth reading.

Why latency matters more than completeness

An agent loop that takes eight seconds per page read becomes unusable long before it becomes incorrect. Static fetching keeps the common case under half a second, which means a research loop can afford to read ten sources instead of two. The rare single page application can be detected cheaply — the extracted text is a tiny fraction of the markup — and only that page pays the headless penalty.

A small example

The whole strategy fits in one conditional, as the following snippet shows. It is deliberately boring code, and that is exactly the point of it.

$result = $static->fetch($url);
if ($result->looksEmpty()) {
    $result = $chrome->fetch($url);
}

What to keep

  • Fetch statically first, always
  • Measure extracted-text ratio to detect shells
  • Escalate to a real browser only on demonstrated need

For a longer treatment of content extraction itself, see the extraction deep dive, which covers scoring heuristics in detail and benchmarks the popular implementations against a shared corpus of real pages collected over several years of production crawling.
